newsitem.title: UK: Dangerous for UK to keep EMU option open - Redwood.
newsitem.headline: Dangerous for UK to keep EMU option open - Redwood.

text.p: Right-wing "Euro-sceptic" Conservative John Redwood said on Wednesday he still hoped the government would rule out, before the general election, Britain's participation in a single European currency.
He said this week's row in the ruling party showed how dangerous it was to keep an open mind over the issue.

Redwood told BBC radio he accepted Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine's comment, made late on Tuesday, that the government would not change its position on economic and monetary union (EMU) before the election.
"But I think it is quite likely that just before the election campaign, or in the election campaign, they will want to develop the policy," Redwood told BBC radio.

The official line, reaffirmed by Prime Minister John Major after a furore caused by comments by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, is that the government should keep its options open on whether to join the single currency planned for 1999.

But Redwood said: "Whilst it's still possible to say today that they don't have to make up their mind, by the time we get to the general election we'll be very close indeed to them having to make up their mind, and I think the public will expect more guidance on how they'll do so."
Redwood said he was not calling on Clarke to resign.

But he said it was worrying that Clarke, who said on Sunday it would be "pathetic" for Britain not to join the single currency right away, only to change its mind later, had stepped so far out of line with the government's position.

"We've seen this week how dangerous it can be if you leave all the options open because it's then very tempting for one minister or another to just push it a bit further on the airwaves than he should have done and then to lead to public dissension," Redwood, who failed in a challenge to Major's leadership of the Conservative party in July 1995, said.
Another former cabinet minister, David Hunt, contradicted Redwood by saying Britain should not close its EMU options.
"It would be very foolish to close off any of the options now, in particular when we may need to consider them for several years," Hunt, a pro-European, told the same programme. REUTER
